title: How to Open a Bank Account: A Beginner's Guide

body:
Opening your first bank account is one of those adult tasks that feels bigger than it is. In reality, learning how to open a bank account mostly comes down to three things: picking the right type of account, gathering a few documents, and filling out a short application. Most people finish in under an hour, and many finish in about fifteen minutes online.

This guide walks you through the whole thing, step by step. You will see how checking, savings, and student accounts compare, exactly what paperwork to bring, how much money you need to start, and what to set up in your first week so the account actually works for you.

## What Is a Bank Account?

A bank account is a place to keep your money with a bank or credit union, where it stays safe, easy to reach, and separate from the cash in your pocket. You can receive pay, pay bills, send money, and take cash out when you need it. A checking account handles everyday spending, while a savings account holds money you want to leave alone and grow.

You do not need a lot of money to start. Many accounts open with a small deposit, and some student accounts open with nothing at all.

## Checking vs Savings vs Student Accounts

Most first accounts fall into three groups: checking for money that moves, savings for money that sits, and student accounts with lower fees and lower minimums.

| Account type | Best for                                 | Watch out for                                         |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Checking         | Everyday spending, bills, and debit card use | Monthly fees if your balance drops below the minimum      |
| Savings          | Money you want to leave alone and grow       | Some banks limit withdrawals or charge for extra ones     |
| Student          | Students, usually under 24                   | It often converts to a regular account after you graduate |

**Checking accounts** are the workhorse. Your pay lands there, your bills come out of it, and your debit card pulls from it. If you only open one account, make it a checking account. Ask whether the account charges a monthly fee, and what you need to do to avoid it.

**Savings accounts** are where money waits. You earn a small amount of interest, and the money is out of your spending path, which makes it easier to leave alone. A savings account is a natural home for a starter emergency fund. [How to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/) shows how to start with small monthly amounts.

**Student accounts** are worth asking about if you are in school. They usually drop or waive monthly fees and lower the opening deposit. The trade-off is that the perks end. When you graduate or pass the age limit, the bank usually converts the account to a regular one, so read the terms first.

Banks are not your only option. Credit unions offer the same basic accounts and are owned by their members. Compare a bank and a credit union the same way: fees, access, and how you will actually use the account.

## What Do You Need to Open a Bank Account?

Banks have to verify who you are before they open an account. That is a legal requirement, not a personal judgment. Having everything ready before you start is the difference between finishing in one visit and making a second trip.

| What to bring              | Why the bank asks       | Notes                                                                     |
|--------------------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Photo ID                       | To prove who you are        | Driver's license, passport, or state ID                                       |
| Social Security number or ITIN | For identity and tax checks | Needed for accounts that pay interest                                         |
| Proof of address               | To confirm where you live   | Utility bill, lease, or bank statement                                        |
| Second form of ID              | As a backup identity check  | Social Security card, birth certificate, or a bill with your name and address |
| Money for the opening deposit  | To fund the account         | Often $25 to $100, sometimes $0                                            |

The Social Security number question trips up a lot of people. For accounts that pay interest, you need a Social Security number or an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN), because interest is taxable income. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes that without one, you may only be able to open an account that does not pay interest. If you do not have a Social Security number, ask the bank what IDs it accepts.

If you are under 18, you will usually need an adult to open the account with you. The adult brings their own photo ID and signs as a joint owner or custodian. Once you turn 18, you can open an account in your own name.

Opening online works the same way, except you upload photos or scans of your documents instead of handing them to a teller. Use a secure connection, and make sure the photos are sharp and readable before you submit them.

## How to Open a Bank Account in 6 Steps

Here is the whole process, in order. You can do most of it from your couch.

### Step 1: Decide what the account is for

Start with the job the account has to do. If you need somewhere for your pay to land and your bills to come out of, open a checking account. If you want a safe place to park money you will not touch, open a savings account.

### Step 2: Compare a few banks or credit unions

Look at three things: fees, access, and fit. Check the monthly fee and how to avoid it. Check ATM access near home, school, and work, plus whether the bank refunds fees from other banks' ATMs. Check the app, because that is where you will live day to day.

### Step 3: Gather your documents

Use the checklist table above. Put your photo ID, proof of address, Social Security number or ITIN, and opening deposit in one place before you start.

### Step 4: Fill out the application

Online, this is a form: your legal name, date of birth, address, phone, email, and ID number. In person, a banker types the same details in while you watch. Read the account agreement, especially the fee section, before you sign.

### Step 5: Fund the account

You can fund a new account with cash at a branch, a check, a transfer from another account, or a direct deposit from your employer. Some banks ask for the opening deposit right away. Others give you a few days.

### Step 6: Set up the basics

Once the account is open, turn on the features that keep it running smoothly. The first-week checklist near the end of this article covers them all, from direct deposit to low-balance alerts.

## Should You Open Your Account Online or In Person?

Both routes end in the same place. Online is faster and you can do it any time, which suits most people. In person helps when your situation is unusual, for example if you have no Social Security number or no proof of address yet.

If you open online, double-check that you are on the bank's real website or app, not a lookalike page. Type the address yourself instead of clicking a link in a text or email.

## How Much Money Do You Need to Open an Account?

Two numbers matter, and people mix them up. The opening deposit is what you put in to start the account. The minimum balance is what you have to keep in the account to avoid a monthly fee. They are often different amounts.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says you typically need an initial deposit between $25 and $100 to open a savings or checking account. Many student accounts ask for less, and some ask for nothing. If the minimum balance is high, the account can still cost you money even after you open it, so check both numbers before you commit.

A quick example shows why the minimum balance matters. This is an illustration with made-up numbers. Say your account charges a $10 monthly fee unless you keep at least $500 in it. If your balance sits at $300 all month, you pay $120 in fees over a year for an account you barely use.

## Is Your Money Safe? Deposit Insurance

Deposit insurance pays you back if your insured bank or credit union fails. You do not apply for it, and you do not pay for it.

In the United States, the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per FDIC-insured bank, for each account ownership category ([FDIC, Understanding Deposit Insurance](https://FDIC.GOV/resources/deposit-insurance/understanding-deposit-insurance)). Checking and savings accounts in your own name at one bank are added together under that one $250,000 limit. You can check whether a bank is FDIC-insured with the FDIC's BankFind tool.

In the United Kingdom, the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) protects eligible deposits up to 120,000 pounds per person, per institution, for firms that failed after 30 November 2025 ([FSCS, Banks, Building Societies and Credit Unions](https://www.fscs.org.uk/what-we-cover/banks-building-societies/)). Before that date, the limit was 85,000 pounds. Protection limits differ by country and change over time, so check the current limit where you live.

Insurance does not cover investments. Stocks, mutual funds, crypto assets, and annuities are not deposits, even if you bought them through a bank.

## What If Your Application Is Denied?

A denial is annoying, but it is not the end of the road. Banks sometimes check reports about your past checking account history. If negative information in one of those reports caused the denial, you can ask which report the bank used, request a copy of it, and dispute any errors in it.

If the report is accurate, ask the bank about a second-chance account. These accounts are built for people with a rough banking history and usually come with tighter rules, such as no overdrafts. A prepaid card is another fallback the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau mentions, but it is not a bank account, and it does not come with the same protections.

Whatever the reason, do not keep applying at bank after bank in the same week. Find out why the first one was denied, fix what you can, and then apply once more with the facts in hand.

## Your First-Week Setup Checklist

Opening the account is the easy part. These eight steps make it useful.

1. Activate your debit card and set a PIN you will remember.
2. Set up direct deposit with your employer so your pay lands automatically.
3. Download the bank's app and turn on login alerts and low-balance alerts.
4. Set up online bill pay for rent, utilities, or any bill you pay every month.
5. Open or link a savings account and set up a small automatic transfer on payday.
6. Check your first statement line by line to catch mistakes or surprise fees.
7. Write down your account and routing numbers somewhere safe, and never share them in a message or email.
8. Build a simple budget around the new account. [How to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) shows how to give every dollar a job.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How old do you have to be to open a bank account?

In the United States, you can open an account in your own name at 18. Under 18, you usually need an adult to open the account with you as a joint owner or custodian. Rules differ by bank and by country.

### Can I open a bank account without a Social Security number?

Sometimes. Some banks accept a foreign passport or another government ID. But to open an account that pays interest, you generally need a Social Security number or an ITIN, because interest is taxable.

### How long does it take to open a bank account?

Online applications often take 10 to 30 minutes, and many accounts are approved the same day. In person, you can usually walk out with an account the same visit.

### Do I need both a checking and a savings account?

Not at first. A checking account covers daily money. Add a savings account when you have money you want to set aside, even if it is only a small amount each payday.

### Does opening a bank account affect my credit score?

No. A bank account is not a loan, and it does not build credit on its own. Building credit needs accounts that report your payments to the credit bureaus, such as a credit card or a loan. [How to build credit from scratch](/blog/how-to-build-credit-from-scratch/) explains the first steps.

### Can I open a bank account online?

Yes, most banks and credit unions let you apply online. You will need clear photos or scans of your ID and proof of address, plus your Social Security number or ITIN.

## Your Next Step

Pick one bank or credit union, gather your documents, and apply this week. The hardest part is starting. Once the account is open and your pay lands in it, the rest of your money life gets easier.

**Related:** [How to avoid bank fees](/blog/avoid-bank-fees/), [What is a high-yield savings account](/blog/high-yield-savings-account/).

This article is general information, not personal financial advice. Account rules, fees, and deposit insurance limits differ by country and by bank, so check the details for your own situation before you apply.
